common_name: Crested Tongue Fern (Crested Japanese Felt Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in a fast-draining, humus-rich mix over rock, bark, or shallow soil in partial to full shade; like the species it tolerates rock crevices, wood mounts, or use as a low groundcover at tree bases.

directions: Plant in a fast-draining, humus-rich medium over rock, bark, or shallow soil in partial to full shade, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings once established. 'Cristata' is a crested sport of the Japanese felt fern in which the normally simple, undivided, tongue-shaped frond tips repeatedly fork and twist, exposing the small round, cinnamon-colored sori that stud the frond undersides and giving the plant an eccentric, curled silhouette quite different from the straight, paddle-shaped blades of the species. Like ordinary tongue fern, it develops a felted coat of rusty-brown scales and tolerates far more drought than typical finely cut ferns once established, making it a conversation-piece accent for rock walls, tree bases, or shaded containers.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in free-draining, peat-free, humus-rich soil or a hanging-basket mix in partial to full shade; this fern dislikes sitting in wet soil even though it wants regular moisture.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in free-draining, humus-rich, peat-free soil in partial to full shade and water regularly, never allowing the mix to become waterlogged. Native to Kyushu, Taiwan, and parts of China, this fern earns its common names from its thick, fuzzy, pale-green, flattened rhizomes that crawl visibly across the soil or pot surface like caterpillars, topped by soft, light-green, finely cut fronds with a graceful drooping habit and contrasting near-black stipes. The fronds die back in cold winters but the rhizomes persist, resprouting reliably in spring. It is especially effective in hanging baskets, where the trailing rhizomes and arching fronds can spill over the container edge, or as an unusual textural accent in a shaded woodland pot grouping.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade; unlike many Blechnum species, this Japanese native tolerates humid summer heat well.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade. Japanese deer fern is a small, tidy woodland species, closely related to the much larger-ranging Blechnum spicant and sometimes treated as a variety of it, that produces two distinct frond types from a low central crown: arching, once-pinnate sterile fronds that form a neat, ground-hugging rosette, and narrower upright fertile fronds bearing the spore-producing sori. At only 8-12 inches tall and wide, it stays compact and well-mannered at the front of a shaded border or in a woodland rock garden. Notably, it has proven more tolerant of hot, humid summers than most other Blechnum species, which often decline in climates outside the cool, humid Pacific Coast, making it a good option for Southeastern and Mid-Atlantic shade gardens where true deer fern (B. spicant) struggles.
